key_finding: Broad narrative overview showing auto-enrollment and default investment options in DC plans lift short-term participation but can suppress longer-term participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature review; abstract-only, no primary effect sizes reported.
why_it_matters: Frames the shape of the closest analogous (employer-plan) literature on defaults and engagement, useful background but not directly actionable for the consumer app decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
abstract-only, no quantitative effect sizes given
review paper, not primary data
relevance_reason: Broad survey of default-and-engagement tradeoffs in the closest analogous literature (employer retirement plans).

key_finding: Steady-state saving rate gains from auto-enrollment (0.6% of income) and auto-escalation (0.3%) are much smaller than commonly assumed once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawal, and opt-out from escalation are modeled; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults actually escalate on the first date.
methodology: Dynamic structural analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover and withdrawal behavior; abstract-only for full method detail.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's skepticism that the enrollment lift is a vanity metric that shrinks once realistic attrition, opt-out, and withdrawal are accounted for.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a liquid consumer round-up product
U.S. retirement system, different regulatory and liquidity context
relevance_reason: Quantifies how a default-driven enrollment lift erodes over time, the core of the brief's persistence question, in a well-cited recent NBER paper.

key_finding: A nudge shrouding the minimum-payment autopay default cut minimum-only paying by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, since nudged users set autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum or dropped autopay altogether.
methodology: Field experiment with credit card customers, six-month follow-up on payment and enrollment behavior.
why_it_matters: Consumer, self-directed, liquid-product evidence that a default/nudge can move a headline enrollment-like metric without moving the outcome that matters, the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk raised for the round-up feature.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
does not directly test opt-in vs opt-out vs active choice entry design
relevance_reason: Consumer financial nudge experiment showing default-driven behavior change decoupled from substantive outcomes, directly analogous to the enrollment-vs-amount-saved question.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, with the effect strongest when incentives are high, choices are complex, and enrollees lack knowledge of their own status.
methodology: Natural experiment using linked administrative and survey data around a nationwide policy rollout.
why_it_matters: Provides a precise, recent, large-scale default effect estimate with heterogeneity by knowledge and complexity, informing who a default captures passively versus who benefits.
limitations: public pension system, not a consumer app
does not report savings amounts or 6-12 month persistence
relevance_reason: Recent large default-effect estimate with heterogeneity by knowledge/complexity, relevant to who benefits from opt-out design.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, though it durably reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel analysis of 100+ US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: The most direct recent evidence for the persistence question: shows how much a default's apparent lift decays over a medium horizon, and that inequality reduction rather than aggregate savings is the durable effect.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer product
longest horizon reported is 36 months, not directly 6-12 months
relevance_reason: Quantifies attenuation of the default enrollment effect over time, central to whether the enrollment lift persists.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces 'passivity' - inertia at low contribution rates, non-management of accounts, and account churn - undermining claims that participation gains alone demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy analysis and literature synthesis; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States plainly the disengagement/passivity risk the support team raised, and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment prompts) transferable to the round-up feature.
limitations: US retirement system framing, not consumer fintech
abstract gives no primary data or effect sizes
narrative synthesis, not a systematic review
relevance_reason: Directly argues the disengagement/passivity risk the brief's support team raised, with mitigation ideas transferable to the round-up feature.

key_finding: Default nudges on investment risk-taking produce medium-to-large behavioral effects but also lower users' rating of the advice and advisor honesty, especially when the individual ultimately rejects the default; question framing (asking about risky vs. safe amounts) produces smaller shifts.
methodology: Three experiments including a large representative sample across five European countries (n=4207).
why_it_matters: EU experimental evidence on when a financial default reads as manipulative rather than helpful, directly informing the dark-pattern reputational risk and the framing of the round-up multiplier choice.
limitations: wealth-management advice setting, not a banking app round-up feature specifically
single-session experimental ratings, not real enrollment or behavior over time
relevance_reason: EU-based experimental evidence on when a financial default is perceived as manipulative, directly informing the dark-pattern and level-framing decisions.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half remained at the default rate after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset default level strongly anchors the ultimately chosen contribution rate, the foundational evidence base for the anchoring question even though set in an employer plan.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a consumer app
predates current mobile/fintech and EU regulatory context
no publication year given, an older foundational study
relevance_reason: The classic study demonstrating that preset default levels anchor final contribution choices, the foundational work the anchoring literature builds on.

key_finding: Only about 15% of individuals are 'active savers' who respond to subsidies mainly by shifting assets ($0.01 of new saving per $1 of subsidy); the other 85% are passive savers unmoved by incentives but strongly responsive to automatic contributions made on their behalf.
methodology: Population-level administrative data for Denmark (41 million observations) exploiting policy variation in subsidies versus automatic contributions.
why_it_matters: Foundational large-scale evidence for the active-vs-passive distinction underlying the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice decision, showing who defaults actually help versus who they don't.
limitations: tax-advantaged retirement accounts, not a liquid consumer savings feature
Danish administrative/tax context differs from EU app regulatory environment
predates current fintech/app-based savings tools
relevance_reason: Foundational large-scale distinction between active and passive savers underpinning who benefits from automatic contributions vs. active choice, directly informing the distributional-risk question.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (no default, forced decision) increases behavior-change rates, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option performs even better, recommended as a complement to automatic enrollment or a substitute when defaults are infeasible or unethical.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice interventions across savings and health-behavior contexts.
why_it_matters: The origin paper for the 'active choice' entry design the brief is weighing against opt-in/opt-out; its enhanced active choice technique (framing losses in the non-chosen option) is a concrete, transferable method for the onboarding screen.
limitations: some experiments are in medication-adherence rather than financial-savings contexts
older paper (2011), predates app-based fintech and current EU dark-pattern scrutiny
abstract gives no 6-month persistence or engagement data
relevance_reason: Foundational paper introducing and testing 'active choice' and 'enhanced active choice' as alternatives to default enrollment, the specific method being weighed in the entry-design decision.
